title: Bones & Muscles
keyIdea: Inside your body is a skeleton: all your bones joined together. Bones are hard and strong. They hold you up and give your body its shape. Some bones keep soft parts safe: the skull covers the brain, and the ribcage covers the heart and lungs. Muscles are joined to bones. A muscle moves a bone by getting shorter and pulling it. Muscles can only pull, never push, so another muscle pulls the bone back the other way.
familyTip: Go on a bone hunt together: gently feel your skull, the bumps of your spine, your ribs and the long bone in your leg, and say what each one does. Then hold your child's upper arm while they bend and straighten it, so they feel the front muscle get short and fat as it pulls.

visual.caption: Is it a bone or a muscle? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: take the bones out and watch the body flop, build a skeleton, guard the brain, heart and lungs, bend an arm, sort bone or muscle.

kid: Inside you there are lots of bones. All your bones joined together make your skeleton. Bones are hard and strong. They hold you up and give you your shape. With no bones, you would be floppy, like jelly.

Some bones keep soft parts safe. Your skull is like a hard helmet. It keeps your brain safe. Your ribs make a cage round your heart and lungs. Your spine, or backbone, runs down your back and helps you stand up tall.
Muscles are soft and stretchy. They are joined to your bones. To move a bone, a muscle gets short and fat and pulls it. Bend your arm and feel the front of it go hard. That is a muscle pulling.
A muscle can only pull. It can not push. So to make your arm straight again, a muscle at the back of your arm pulls the other way. Your heart is a muscle too. It squeezes all day and all night.
adult: Ages 5 to 7. This builds the National Curriculum in England Year 1 aim to identify, name, draw and label the basic parts of the human body, and leads into Year 3 animals including humans: humans have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement. NGSS 4-LS1-1 later asks how internal structures support survival. Key words: bone, skeleton, skull, ribcage, ribs, spine (backbone), joint, muscle, pull, support, protect.

An adult skeleton has about 206 bones; a newborn has around 270 to 300 that later fuse. The skull protects the brain, the ribcage protects the heart and lungs, and the spine supports the body and protects the spinal cord. Skeletal muscles are joined to bones by tendons and move them only by contracting (pulling). They work in pairs: the biceps bends the elbow and the triceps straightens it. The heart is a different kind of muscle, called cardiac muscle.

Common mistakes: thinking bones are not alive or do nothing but sit there; thinking muscles push as well as pull; thinking the skeleton is one big bone or only the bones you can feel; putting the brain under the ribs or the heart in the skull; and calling the heart a bone because it sits inside the ribcage. The lab, the practice and the challenge target each of these.

In the lab your child takes the bones out of a body and watches it flop, then puts them back; drags the skull, ribcage, spine, arm bones and leg bones into place; gives the brain, heart and lungs the bone that keeps each one safe; drags a hand to bend an arm and sees the front muscle shorten and bulge, then the back muscle pull it straight; and sorts six cards into bone or muscle.

practice.prompt: What would your body be like with no bones?
practice.hint: What holds you up and gives you your shape?
practice.explain: Bones hold you up. With no bones, your body could not keep its shape and would flop down.

practice.prompt: You bend your arm {n} times and make it straight {n} times. Each move is one muscle pull. How many pulls is that?
practice.hint: Bending is one pull. Making it straight is another pull, by a different muscle.
practice.explain: {n} bends and {n} straightens make {=2*n} pulls. Every move is a muscle pulling, never pushing.

practice.prompt: Which bone keeps your brain safe?
practice.hint: Your brain is in your head. Which bone is like a helmet?
practice.explain: The skull is the hard bone round your brain, like a helmet.

practice.prompt: A skeleton puzzle has {n} bones. You have put {k} in place. How many bones are left to put in?
practice.hint: Take the bones you have placed away from all the bones.
practice.explain: {n} take away {k} leaves {=n-k} bones to put in. All the bones together make the skeleton.

practice.prompt: How does a muscle move a bone?
choices: It gets short and pulls the bone
practice.hint: Bend your arm. Does the front of it get short and fat, or long and thin?
practice.explain: A muscle gets short and fat and pulls the bone. Muscles can only pull.

pool.prompt: What do we call all your bones joined together?
pool.hint: It is the word for the whole frame of bones inside you.
pool.explain: All your bones joined together make your skeleton.

pool.prompt: Which bones keep your heart and lungs safe?
pool.hint: Your heart and lungs are in your chest. Feel the bumpy bones there.
pool.explain: Your ribs make a cage round your heart and lungs, so we call it the ribcage.

pool.prompt: Can a muscle push a bone?
pool.hint: Think of the arm in the lab. Which muscle made it straight again?
pool.explain: Muscles only pull. A different muscle pulls the other way to make your arm straight.

pool.prompt: Is your heart a bone or a muscle?
pool.hint: Your heart squeezes to pump blood. Can a hard bone squeeze?
pool.explain: Your heart is a muscle. It squeezes all day and night. The ribs round it are bones.

pool.prompt: Your ribs come in pairs, one on each side. A model shows {n} pairs. How many ribs is that?
pool.hint: A pair is 2. Count 2 for each pair.
pool.explain: {n} pairs of ribs is {=2*n} ribs. Most people have 12 pairs, which is 24 ribs.

choices: Down the middle of your back
pool.hint: It is also called the backbone.
pool.explain: The spine, or backbone, runs down the middle of your back and helps you stand tall.

pool.prompt: What happens to the front muscle in your arm when you bend it?
choices: It turns hard like a bone
pool.hint: Feel the front of your arm as you bend it.
pool.explain: The muscle gets short and fat as it pulls. It feels hard, but it is still a soft muscle, not a bone.

pool.hint: What do muscles pull on to move you?
pool.explain: Muscles are joined to bones. When they pull, the bones move.

pool.prompt: Your skeleton puzzle has a skull, a ribcage and a spine. You add {n} more bones. How many bones are in your puzzle now?
pool.hint: Count the skull, the ribcage and the spine first. That is 3. Then add the new bones.
pool.explain: 3 bones and {n} more make {=3+n} bones. Every bone you add is part of the skeleton.
